unit.why: A short anecdote: a father comes to the Rebbe of Apta about his son, who is about to apostatize, and the rebbe answers with a condition and a verse-based explanation.

stories.summary_en: A man asks the Rebbe of Apta to help turn back his son, who has abandoned religion and wants to convert. The rebbe says the son can be saved only if he has not eaten chametz on Pesach since he lapsed, and links this to the juxtaposed verses in Ki Tisa.

quotes: בן שנתפקר ורצה להמיר דתו ר"ל
tags.why: The son's threatened apostasy is the subject

quotes: וביקש מהרב לעזור לו להפוך לבו לטוב
tags.why: The tzaddik judges whether a sinner can be brought back

quotes: פ"א בא לפני הרב מאפטא איש א׳
tags.why: A petitioner comes before the rebbe with a request

quotes: אז אפשר להושיעו. ואם לאו לאו
tags.why: The request is for spiritual repair of the son, and the rebbe sets its condition

quotes: שלא אכל חמץ בפסח מעת שנתפקר
tags.why: Keeping the chametz prohibition is the criterion for whether the son can be saved
The possibility of the son's return is at issue

quotes: ב׳ כתובים בפ' כי תשא אלהי מסכה לא תעשה לך
tags.why: The answer is backed by exegesis of juxtaposed verses
Pesach is central to the answer, though the story is not set on it
Borderline: father and son are central, but they are not the tzaddik's family
The anecdote is thin and serves an exegetical point

missing_concepts: link between keeping Pesach/chametz and remaining within Judaism (a residual mitzvah as an anchor against apostasy)
father's intercession for a wayward child
